items.title: SightPress documentation
items.text:
SightPress is a powerful content management system (CMS) for everyone, designed with blind and low-vision creators and audiences in mind. It is built on modern, object-oriented PHP and is free software, licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later.

With SightPress you can run many websites from one installation, each in as many languages as you need. The admin area, the default theme and every built-in feature aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. Every task works with a keyboard alone and with a screen reader.

items.title: Status
items.text: This is the first version of SightPress (0.1). You can create websites from the command line, and each website has ready-made pages, an admin panel to write and publish pages through review, a media library, menus, invitations, site settings and an audit log. Every page is ready for search engines and AI readers.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• To see what SightPress can do, with ideas for websites, read What you can build.
  • The source code lives on GitHub in the SightPress organisation.
  • To run SightPress on your own computer, follow Getting started.
  • To make a theme of your own, follow the tutorial Create a theme.
  • The how-to guides show you how to do one task at a time, such as creating a website or writing and publishing a page.
  • The reference pages explain roles and permissions, blocks, search and AI visibility and the command line tool.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
This guide shows you how to run SightPress on your own computer, create your first website and sign in to its admin panel, so that you can try it out. You don't need to know how to program. It takes about 30 minutes, most of which is waiting for downloads.

What you can try today

You can create a website with ready-made pages, write, schedule and publish pages, translate them into other languages, upload pictures and other files, invite people or let them sign up, make pages members-only, search the website, read its visitor statistics, turn features on or off, change its theme, colours and page layouts, add captions and transcripts, keep files in the cloud, and set up an optional AI assistant with your own key. Running SightPress on a public server is not covered yet.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A computer running Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux.
  • About 5 GB of free disk space.
  • An internet connection.
  • Permission to install programs on the computer.

You type some commands in a terminal. A terminal is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking:

  • On Windows, open Windows Terminal or PowerShell from the Start menu.
  • On macOS, open Terminal from Applications, then Utilities.
  • On Linux, open your terminal app.

Type or paste each command, then press Enter.

items.title: Step 1: install Docker
items.text:
Docker runs SightPress and everything it needs inside separate, self-contained boxes called containers. You don't have to install PHP, a web server or a database yourself.

  1. Install Docker:
    • On Windows or macOS, install Docker Desktop. On Windows, accept the option to use WSL 2 if the installer asks.
    • On Linux, install Docker Engine and the Docker Compose plugin.
  2. On Windows or macOS, open Docker Desktop and wait until it says that Docker is running.

  3. In the terminal, type:

    docker compose version

    You should see a line such as Docker Compose version v5.3.0. The number may be different. If you see "command not found" or a similar message, Docker is not installed correctly, or Docker Desktop is not running.

items.title: Step 2: install Git
items.text:
Git downloads the SightPress files from GitHub, where they are published.

  1. Install Git from the Git downloads page. On macOS, you can instead type git --version in the terminal and accept the offer to install the developer tools.

  2. In the terminal, type:

    git --version

    You should see a line such as git version 2.51.0.

items.title: Step 3: download SightPress
items.text:
You only download the skeleton, the project you start. The other parts of SightPress are fetched for you automatically the first time you start it, in step 4.

  1. Make a folder for SightPress and go into it:

    mkdir sightpress
cd sightpress

  2. Download the skeleton:

    git clone https://github.com/sightpress/skeleton.git

    You should see a few lines that end with done.

  3. Go into the skeleton folder:

    cd skeleton

Only on Linux

The SightPress container writes files as user number 1000. If your Linux user has a different number, files can end up owned by the wrong user. Type id -u. If it shows anything other than 1000, copy the settings file with cp .env.example .env, open .env in a text editor, and set UID and GID to the numbers that id -u and id -g show. Windows and macOS users can skip this.

items.title: Step 4: start SightPress
items.text:
1. In the skeleton folder, type:

    docker compose up

  2. Wait. The first time, Docker downloads and builds everything it needs. This can take 5 to 15 minutes. You see many lines of text scroll past. Later starts take a few seconds.

  3. SightPress is ready when the text stops scrolling and you see lines starting with php-1 that end with ready to handle connections.

Leave this terminal window open. SightPress stops when you close it.

items.title: Step 5: open SightPress in your browser
items.text:
1. Open your web browser and go to http://localhost:8080.
  2. You should see a plain page with the heading No site configured and this text: "SightPress is running, but no site is set up for this address yet. If you look after this server, create a site and link this address to it." The browser tab is called "No site configured - SightPress".

This is the right result. It means SightPress is running, but has no website yet. You create one in the next steps.

If the browser shows 502 Bad Gateway, SightPress is still finishing its first start. Wait a minute, then reload the page.

items.title: Step 6: make a settings file with a secret key
items.text:
SightPress keeps its settings in a file called .env in the skeleton folder. One setting, the secret key, protects the address of each website's database. You make it once.

  1. Open a second terminal window and go to the skeleton folder, as in step 3. Leave the first window running.

  2. Copy the example settings file:

    cp .env.example .env

  3. Make a secret key:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php php -r 'echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32)), PHP_EOL;'

    You should see one line of 64 letters and digits, such as 3f9a…. Yours will be different.

  4. Open the .env file in a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on macOS. Find the line APP_SECRET= and paste your key straight after the = sign, with no spaces. Save the file.

  5. Keep a copy of the key somewhere safe, such as a password manager. Without it, SightPress can't open your websites' databases.
  6. Go back to the first terminal window and press Ctrl+C to stop SightPress. Then start it again with docker compose up, so that it reads the new settings.

The copied file also turns on the test e-mail inbox, which catches every e-mail SightPress sends. See Open the test e-mail inbox.

items.title: Step 7: create your first website
items.text:
1. In the second terminal window, type this command on one line. Change the e-mail address and the names to your own if you like. (You can also type just docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create and answer one question at a time: see Create a website.)

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create demo --domain=localhost --db=sqlite:////app/sites/demo.sqlite --url=http://localhost:8080 --owner-type=organization --locale=en-GB --name="Riverside Library" --admin-email=ada@example.org --admin-first-name=Ada --admin-last-name=Lovelace

  2. After a few seconds, you should see lines like these:

    Getting the SQLite file /app/sites/demo.sqlite ready…
Ran 25 database migrations.
Created the account of the first admin, Ada Lovelace (ada@example.org).
Set up the roles admin, editor, contributor and member.
Gave the first admin the admin role.
Give the setup code 388 641 to ada@example.org. They go to http://localhost:8080/login/setup, type their email address and the code, and choose their password. The code works once, for 7 days.
Made the site's icons, wordmark and share image from its name; replace them with site:branding:set.
Published the starter pages in British English: Welcome to Riverside Library, About us, Contact us, Privacy notice, Terms of use, Accessibility statement.
Added 5 starter pages to the main and footer menus.
The site "demo" is ready at http://localhost:8080.

  3. Write down the setup code, the six digits after "Give the setup code". Yours will be different. You need it in the next step.

Create a website explains every part of the command.

items.title: Step 8: choose your password and sign in
items.text:
1. In your browser, go to http://localhost:8080/login/setup. You should see the heading Set up your account.
  2. In Email address, type the address you used, for example ada@example.org.
  3. In 6-digit code, type the setup code. You can type it with or without the space.
  4. Choose Continue. You should see the heading Choose your password.
  5. In New password, type a password of at least 12 characters. A few unrelated words make a strong password that is easy to remember.
  6. Choose Set password. You should see the sign-in page with the message "Your password has been set. Sign in with it now."
  7. Type your e-mail address and your new password, then choose Sign in.
  8. You should see the admin panel's Dashboard. The browser tab says "Dashboard - Admin - Riverside Library". The admin menu has links such as Dashboard, Pages, Analytics, Redirects, Media, Menus, People, Invite someone, Site settings, Features and Audit log.

SightPress never sends links to sign in or to set a password. It always gives you a code to type on the website instead. See Codes we send you.

items.title: Step 9: look at your website
items.text:
1. Go to http://localhost:8080.
  2. You should see the home page, with the heading Welcome to Riverside Library, a main menu with About us and Contact us, and a footer menu with the privacy notice, the terms of use and the accessibility statement.

Every new website starts with these six pages, already published. Change them in the admin panel under Pages. See Write and publish a page.

The pages follow your computer's light or dark setting, and every page works with a keyboard alone and with a screen reader. While SightPress runs on your computer, every page asks search engines not to list it.

items.title: Step 10: stop SightPress
items.text:
1. Go back to the terminal window where SightPress is running.
  2. Press Ctrl+C. You should see lines that end with Stopped.

To start SightPress again later, go to the skeleton folder and type docker compose up again. Your website and your account are kept.

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: "port is already allocated" or "address already in use" Another program on your computer is using one of the ports SightPress needs. See Change the ports SightPress uses. "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" Docker is not running. On Windows or macOS, open Docker Desktop and wait until it says that Docker is running. On Linux, type sudo systemctl start docker. The page doesn't load at all Check that the terminal still shows SightPress running, and that the address is exactly http://localhost:8080, with http, not https. "APP_SECRET is not set" when you create the site The secret key is missing from .env. Go back to step 6. The website shows an error page after you created it SightPress was not restarted after you added the secret key. Stop it with Ctrl+C and start it again with docker compose up. "This code doesn't work" on the setup page Check the e-mail address and the six digits. A setup code works once, for 7 days. To get a new one, see Create a website.

items.title: What to do next
items.text:
The how-to guides show you how to write and publish pages, add a language and translate a page, schedule, move or restore pages, make a site members-only, let people sign up, turn features on or off, search the website, read its analytics, set up the AI assistant and run SightPress in the background. To move an older installation to this version, see Update SightPress.

To start your website in more than one language, give site:create a list in --locale, for example --locale=en-GB,pt-PT: every starter page is then written in each language. See Add a language and translate a page to add one later, and Turn features on or off to choose the optional features.

You can help improve SightPress without being a developer: see Report a problem and the other guides under Help improve SightPress.

To change how your website looks, see Install and change a theme and Choose a page layout. Your files are kept in the sites folder on your computer. To keep them elsewhere, see Keep your files in the cloud. For big files, see Upload large files and Import files from a folder. To make videos and recordings accessible, see Add captions and transcripts.

The reference pages explain roles, blocks, search and AI visibility and the command line tool.

items.title: What you can build with SightPress
items.text:
SightPress is a content management system (CMS): a program that lets you build and run websites without writing code. You write pages in an admin panel, and SightPress turns them into a website that everyone can use, including people who use a screen reader, a keyboard alone or screen magnification.

This page explains what SightPress can do today, then gives you ideas for websites you could build with it.

items.title: What you can do today
items.text: SightPress is still at an early stage, and this page follows the newest documentation. Features marked next release are finished but aren't in version 0.3 yet. SightPress already gives you the following.

items.title: Run many websites from one installation
items.text: One installation of SightPress can run as many websites as you need. Each website has its own pages, people, files, menus and settings, and its own main language. A person can be an editor on one website and a contributor on another. See Create a website.

items.title: Write pages with blocks
items.text:
A page is a list of blocks, such as a heading, some text or a picture. There are ten kinds:

Block What it is for Heading Starting a part of the page. Text Paragraphs, lists, links, quotes and more. Image One picture, with its alternative text and a caption. Gallery A set of up to 50 pictures. Video A video with captions and a transcript. It never starts by itself. Audio A sound recording, such as a podcast episode, with a transcript. File download A file such as a PDF, with its type and size shown in the link. Call to action A button that leads somewhere, such as "Book a visit". Columns Two to four columns side by side on wide screens. Contact form A form visitors use to send you a message, without a puzzle to solve.

Every block is described in Blocks.

items.title: Publish with confidence
items.text:
• Accessibility checks. Before a page is published, SightPress checks it. A picture with no alternative text, a video with speech but no captions or text that is too faint to read stops the page from being published until it is fixed. Smaller problems, such as a link that says "click here", come up as suggestions.
  • Review before publishing. Contributors write pages and send them for review. Editors and admins approve and publish them. See Write and publish a page.
  • Roles for your team. Admins, editors, contributors and members each see and do only what they need. See Roles and permissions.
  • An audit log. Admins can see who changed what, and when.

items.title: Look after your files and people
items.text:
• A media library for pictures, videos, sound recordings, captions files and documents. Visitors only see the files you publish.
  • Invitations. Invite people by e-mail. They get a 6-digit code, never a link. See Codes we send you.
  • Menus. A main menu and a footer menu, which you change in the admin panel.
  • Site settings. The website's name, profile, logo and other details.

items.title: Be found in search engines and AI search
items.text: Every public page is ready for search engines and for AI search engines and assistants, with nothing to set up: a title and description, a sitemap, structured data and a plain-text version of each page. You choose whether AI services may read your pages. See Search and AI visibility.

items.title: Do every task with a keyboard and a screen reader
items.text: The admin panel, the default theme and every built-in feature aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. Nothing depends on dragging, on colour alone or on a puzzle to prove you are human. Admins can also do many tasks with the command line tool.

items.title: Reach more people and understand your visitors
items.text:
• Several languages. Publish a website in more than one language. See Add a language and translate a page.
  • Site search. Visitors can search your pages. See Search your website.
  • Analytics. See how many people visit and what they read. See See who visits your website.
  • An AI assistant. Turn it on if you want help drafting, with your own API key. A person checks every suggestion. See Use the AI assistant.

items.title: Choose how your website looks and where its files live
items.text:
• Themes and colours. Install other themes, and change the colours on the Appearance screen. See Install and change a theme.
  • Large files. Send big files in parts, and pause or resume them. See Upload large files.
  • Cloud storage and a CDN. Keep a website's files with an S3-compatible service, and deliver public files from near each visitor.

items.title: Ideas for websites
items.text: These ideas use only what SightPress can do today. Each one lists the blocks and features that help most.

items.title: A website for a small business
items.text:
A café, a hairdresser, a plumber or a shop that wants people to find it and get in touch.

  • Pages: Home, What we offer, Prices, About us, Contact.
  • A Gallery of your work or your premises, and a Call to action such as "Book an appointment" that opens a phone number or an e-mail address.
  • A Contact form, so that customers can write to you without seeing your e-mail address.
  • Search and AI visibility, so that people asking a search engine or an AI assistant can find you.

items.title: A charity or community group
items.text:
A charity, a residents' association, a sports club or a support group.

  • Pages: Who we are, What we do, Get involved, Annual reports, Contact.
  • File download blocks for annual reports, minutes and leaflets, with their type and size shown.
  • A Video about your work, with captions and a transcript, so that everyone can follow it.
  • Roles, so that volunteers write pages as contributors and a trustee publishes them as an editor.

items.title: A podcast or audio project
items.text:
A podcast, an audio drama, a radio show or a collection of oral history recordings.

  • One page per episode, with an Audio block and its transcript. The transcript makes every episode readable and searchable.
  • A File download for show notes or extra material.
  • A page for each guest or contributor, with an Image and a short biography.

items.title: A portfolio
items.text:
An artist, photographer, writer, musician or designer who wants to show their work.

  • A Gallery for each project, with alternative text that describes every picture. Writing good alternative text helps blind and low-vision visitors enjoy your work, and helps search engines understand it.
  • Columns to put a picture next to its description on wide screens.
  • Audio or Video blocks for performances and recordings.
  • A Contact form for commissions and bookings.

items.title: A school, library or museum
items.text:
A school, a public library, a museum or a gallery that must be accessible to everyone.

  • Pages: Visit us, Opening hours, What's on, Accessibility, Contact.
  • Video tours with captions, and Audio guides with transcripts.
  • File download blocks for policies, timetables and forms.
  • Roles, so that staff in different departments write their own pages, and a web editor approves them.
  • One installation with a separate website for each school, branch or venue.

items.title: An accessibility-first information website
items.text:
A council service, a health clinic, a disability organisation or a guide to a local service, where clear, accessible information matters most.

  • Short pages with clear Headings, so that screen reader users can jump from part to part.
  • File download blocks for forms and leaflets, plus the same information as a page, so that nobody has to open a PDF.
  • The accessibility checks stop common mistakes, such as a missing caption, before they reach the public.

items.title: A personal website or blog-style journal
items.text:
A personal homepage, a CV or a journal of your projects, travels or hobbies.

  • Pages: About me, Projects, CV, Contact.
  • A File download for your CV as a PDF.
  • One page per project or trip, with Images, a Gallery and Text.

items.title: Several websites for an agency or organisation
items.text:
A web agency, a federation of clubs or an organisation with several brands.

  • One installation of SightPress with a website for each client, club or brand, each with its own domain, language, people and settings.
  • Each website keeps its own roles, so that each client or club looks after its own content.
  • The command line tool to create and list websites quickly.

items.title: Coming later
items.text: Later versions of SightPress add more, such as add-on modules and a guide to putting SightPress on a public server. The Getting started guide and the how-to guides are updated as each feature arrives.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• To decide which options and content suit your website, read Plan your website.
  • To try SightPress on your own computer, follow Getting started.
  • To build your first website, follow Create a website, then Write and publish a page.

items.title: How-to guides
items.text: Each guide shows you how to do one thing with SightPress, in short, numbered steps. They assume you have already followed Getting started, so SightPress is downloaded and runs on your computer.

items.title: Your website
items.text:
• Plan your website: choose the right options and content for what you need.
  • Create a website with the command line tool, and give its first admin a setup code.
  • Write and publish a page, from a draft through review to the public website.
  • Schedule a page to be published, or taken off the website, at a set time.
  • Restore an older version of a page, and see what changed, word by word.
  • Move or rename a page without breaking links, and look after the redirects.
  • Put a page in the trash and get it back, archive it, copy it or delete it for good.
  • Add a language and translate a page.
  • Make a website or a page members-only.
  • Let people sign up for an account, confirmed with an emailed code.
  • Turn features on or off for one website, and delete a feature's data.
  • Install and change a theme: install themes on the server, and choose one for each website.
  • Choose a page layout: home, standard, landing, sidebar or full width.
  • Add captions and transcripts to videos and recordings, in each language.
  • Search your website from any page, and leave a page out of the search.
  • See who visits your website: the Analytics screen, its charts and tables, and what is and isn't counted.

items.title: Your account
items.text: • Change your email address or password on My account.

items.title: Running SightPress
items.text:
• Update SightPress to a newer version, keeping every website.

  • Keep your files in the cloud: AWS, Cloudflare or another service, with a CDN.

  • Upload large files: send big files in parts, and pause, resume or cancel.
  • Import files from a folder on the server, of any size.
  • Fix upload size limits: what the admin warning means, and how to let larger files in.
  • Choose upload limits: how large a file each website accepts.
  • Run SightPress in the background, so that you can close the terminal.
  • Change the ports SightPress uses, if another program already uses them.
  • Start a database server: MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL.

items.title: Checking the built-in tools
items.text:
• Open the test e-mail inbox, which catches every e-mail SightPress sends.
  • Open the file storage console, a local service for trying cloud storage.
  • Try the command line tool.

items.title: Signing in
items.text: • Codes we send you: why SightPress never sends links, and how to type a 6-digit code.

items.title: Help improve SightPress
items.text:
You don't need to be a developer for any of these. Everyone who takes part follows our Code of Conduct.

  • Report a problem, including accessibility barriers, with or without a GitHub account.
  • Translate SightPress into a language you speak fluently.
  • Review the interface as a sighted person, and describe a screenshot in words.
  • Review a theme change from the preview every theme pull request gets.
  • Test with assistive technology before each release.

items.title: Add a language and translate a page
items.text:
A website can be written in several languages. Each page then has one translation per language, with its own title, address and content. Visitors read the page in their language, and search engines are told which pages are translations of each other.

You need to be an admin to add a language, and an editor or admin to publish a translation. Contributors can write translations; an editor publishes them.

items.title: Add a language
items.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel, for example at http://localhost:8080/admin.
  2. Choose Site settings in the admin menu, then Change the languages. You should see the heading Languages and a table of the languages of the site, the main language first.
  3. Under Add a language, in Language to add, choose the language, for example Spanish (es). You can type the first letters of its name to move through the list.
  4. Choose Add language. You should see the message "Added Spanish. Translate pages into it from each page’s editor." and Spanish in the table.

Pages in the main language have addresses without a language part, such as /about. Pages in the other languages start with the language code in lower case, such as /es/about.

items.title: Start with the ready-made pages
items.text:
New websites come with six starter pages (home, About, Contact, Privacy, Terms and Accessibility). To get them in the new language too:

  1. On the Languages screen, choose Create the starter pages in Spanish.
  2. Each starter page gets a Spanish translation, as a draft. Nothing is published until you publish each translation (see below).

When SightPress has no ready-made text in that language, the drafts are written in British English for you to translate, and a message says so.

items.title: Translate a page
items.text:
1. Choose Pages in the admin menu, then the page, for example About us.
  2. In the page editor, go to the Translations section. It lists each language of the site with the state of the page in it: Not written yet, Draft, Draft translation, Published, or Drafted by the AI assistant, not checked yet.
  3. Next to Spanish, choose Translate into Spanish from British English. This copies the title, address and blocks into a new Spanish draft and opens it. The British English page doesn't change.
  4. Translate the title, the address (for example sobre-nosotros), the summary and every block, then choose Save page.

Let the AI assistant draft it

If the AI assistant is on, Draft a translation into Spanish with the AI assistant writes a first draft for you, block by block. It is marked Drafted by the AI assistant, not checked yet until a person saves a change or chooses I checked this translation, and can't be published before that. See Use the AI assistant.

items.title: Publish the translation
items.text:
1. In the Spanish translation's editor, choose Publish this translation. The same checks run as for any page: for example, every picture needs a description in Spanish.
  2. If a check fails, a list at the top says what to fix. Fix it, save, and publish again.
  3. You should see the message "Published the Spanish translation. Visitors can see it now." and Published next to Spanish in the Translations section.

Visitors see a translation only when both the page and the translation are published. A draft translation is not in the menus, the sitemap or the language links that search engines read.

items.title: Check it on the website
items.text:
1. Go to the page in its new language, for example http://localhost:8080/es/sobre-nosotros.
  2. You should see the page in Spanish. The menus use the Spanish titles, and the language switcher lists each language in its own words, such as "Español".
  3. Someone whose browser asks for a language when they open the home page is taken to the home page in that language, or the closest one: for example Brazilian Portuguese to European Portuguese, and otherwise the main language.

Pictures can have their description, caption and transcript in each language: open the picture in Media and fill in the fields for each language. When a language has none, the main language's text is used, never nothing.

items.title: Change the main language or remove a language
items.text:
• Make Spanish the main language changes the addresses of the pages in the old and the new main language. Links to their old addresses stop working, so do this early, before the website is public.
  • Remove Spanish asks you to confirm on its own page. The Spanish translations are kept but can't be read. Adding Spanish again brings them back. People who chose Spanish for their emails get the main language instead.

items.title: With the command line tool
items.text:
In the skeleton folder, replace demo with the short name of your website:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:add demo es
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:default demo es
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:remove demo es --yes

Without --yes, site:locale:remove only explains what would happen. To start a website in several languages, give site:create a list, such as --locale=en-GB,pt-PT,es: every starter page is then written in each of them.

items.title: Add captions and transcripts
items.text: Captions show the words and important sounds of a video as it plays. A transcript gives the same information as text that anyone can read, including people using a screen reader or a braille display. SightPress asks for them before a page with a video or recording can be published.

items.title: Add captions to a video
items.text:
Captions are a WebVTT file, with a name ending in .vtt. Many video and subtitle tools can export one.

  1. In the admin menu, choose Media, then open the video.
  2. Find the Captions heading. There is one file field per language of the website.
  3. Choose the file under Captions file in …, then choose Upload captions in ….
  4. You should see "The captions have been saved." If the file has a mistake, it is refused with the line to fix, for example "line 3: the cue must end after it starts".

Visitors get a captions choice per language in the video player. It starts on the language of the page, or else the website's main language.

items.title: Write a transcript
items.text:
1. In Media, open the video or recording.
  2. Write the transcript for each language. Include who is speaking and any important sounds.
  3. Choose Save details.

Visitors open it with the Transcript button under the player, by mouse or keyboard. Transcripts of public files are also in each page's Markdown version and in llms-full.txt, for AI readers.

A video with no speech

A video with no speech still needs a description of what happens in its transcript.

items.title: Tidy a transcript with the AI assistant
items.text:
If the AI assistant is on, it can add punctuation, paragraphs and speaker labels to a saved transcript of up to 6,000 characters. It can't change the words: an answer that does is refused.

  1. Choose Tidy up the transcript, then Insert.
  2. Read the result against the recording, and correct it.
  3. Tick I checked the transcript against the recording, then choose Save details.

Until someone has checked it, pages that show it can't be published.

items.title: Privacy
items.text: Captions and transcripts can name or quote people. They are deleted with the file.

items.title: Change the ports SightPress uses
items.text: A port is a numbered door on your computer that a program listens on. Each address SightPress uses ends in a port number, such as the 8080 in http://localhost:8080. If another program already uses one of these ports, SightPress can't start and you see an error such as "port is already allocated". This guide shows you how to choose different ports.

items.title: The ports SightPress uses
items.text:
Setting Default What it is for HTTP_PORT 8080 SightPress itself MAILPIT_UI_PORT 8025 The test e-mail inbox MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT 1025 Where the test e-mail inbox receives e-mail MINIO_API_PORT 9000 File storage MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT 9001 The file storage console

The error message names the port that is taken, for example 127.0.0.1:8080.

items.title: Change a port
items.text:
1. If SightPress is running, stop it. See Run SightPress in the background, or press Ctrl+C in the terminal where it runs.

  2. In the skeleton folder, check whether a file called .env exists. If it doesn't, create it by copying the example file:

    cp .env.example .env

    On Windows in PowerShell, cp works too.

  3. Open .env in a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on macOS. The name starts with a dot, so some file browsers hide it; you can open it from the editor's Open menu instead.

  4. Find the line for the port you want to change, for example HTTP_PORT=8080, and change the number, for example to HTTP_PORT=8081. Pick a number between 1024 and 65535 that no other program uses.
  5. Save the file.
  6. Start SightPress again with docker compose up.
  7. Use the new number in the address. With HTTP_PORT=8081, go to http://localhost:8081. You should see the No site configured page.

items.title: Who can reach these ports
items.text: Every port listens only on your own computer (the address 127.0.0.1, also called localhost). Other computers on your network can't reach SightPress.

items.title: Change your email address or password
items.text: Everyone with an account on a website, members included, can change their own details on My account.

items.title: Open My account
items.text:
Sign in, then choose My account: in the admin panel it is a link in the header; on the website, go to /account, for example http://localhost:8080/account.

On My account you can also change your name, display name, time zone, language (on websites in several languages) and profile picture. People who use the admin panel can choose Reduce motion and Larger text there.

items.title: Change your password
items.text:
1. On My account, choose Change your password.
  2. In Current password, type the password you use now.
  3. In New password, type a new one. The rules are written under the field.
  4. Choose Change password. You should see "Your password has been changed. You are still signed in here, and signed out everywhere else."

If the current password is wrong, a message at the top of the page says so. After five wrong tries in 15 minutes, you have to wait, as when signing in.

items.title: Change your email address
items.text:
1. On My account, choose Change your email address.
  2. Type the New email address and your Current password, then choose Send the code.
  3. We email a 6-digit code to the new address. The email has no link.
  4. Type the code on the next page and choose Confirm my new email address. You should see "Your email address is now …. Sign in with it from now on."

Your old address gets an email saying that the address was changed, with the new one partly hidden and no link. Until you type the code, nothing changes. See Codes we send you.

Every change is written to the website's audit log, without the passwords.

items.title: Choose a page layout
items.text:
A layout decides how a page's content is arranged. You choose one for each page. Your words and blocks stay the same when you change it.

  1. In the admin menu, choose Pages, then open a page, or choose to add a new one.
  2. Find Layout and choose one.
  3. Save the page, then open it to check how it reads.
Layout What it does Good for Home page The title and summary as a large introduction. The first page of the website. Standard page One comfortable reading column. Most pages. Landing A wide introduction band, then content in full-width sections. A single campaign or call to action. Sidebar Content with a side column of related links and notes. It lists the pages in the same section. A section with several related pages. Full width Content across the whole page width. Wide galleries and tables.

On narrow screens and when zoomed in, every layout becomes one column, so nothing needs sideways scrolling.

items.title: When you change theme
items.text: Not every theme has every layout. Before you switch to a theme that lacks one, the Appearance screen lists the pages affected. They are shown in the standard layout, and they keep their own layout for when you switch back. See Install and change a theme.

items.title: Choose upload limits
items.text: This guide helps whoever runs a SightPress installation decide how large a file each website accepts. A brochure website might keep small pictures and no large videos, while a podcast needs long audio files.

items.title: The two kinds of limit
items.text:
• Website limits say how large a picture, video, audio file or document can be. Each website can have its own.
  • Server limits say how much the server takes in one upload. They are the same for every website. If you need to change them, see Fix upload size limits.

People can upload the smaller of the two. Website admins see the result in Site settings and next to each upload field, but they can't change it.

items.title: Recommended values
items.text:
Kind of installation UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT Website limits Standard (the default) 64M 256M Pictures 20 MB, documents 50 MB, audio 200 MB, video 1 GB Small or shared hosting 32M 256M Pictures 20 MB, documents 20 MB, audio and video 32 MB Lots of media 64M 512M Larger audio and video, and pictures up to 50 million pixels

With JavaScript, SightPress sends large files in parts, so a file can be larger than UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE, up to the website's limit. Without JavaScript, a file can't be larger than UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE.

items.title: See a website's limits
items.text:
Type this in the skeleton folder, replacing demo with the website's short name:

docker compose exec php bin/sightpress site:media:limits demo

You should see each kind of file, its limit, and whether it is this site's own value or the install default.

items.title: Change a website's limits
items.text:
1. Lowering a limit needs no preparation. To raise one above the default, first set the most any website may use in config/tenant.php:

    'media' => [
    'limits' => [
        'max' => ['audio' => '500M'],
    ],
],

  2. Set the website's limit:

    docker compose exec php bin/sightpress site:media:limits demo --audio=500M

    You should see The upload limits of "demo" have been saved. A value above the maximum is refused, and the message says what the maximum is.

  3. Find out which server values that limit needs:

    docker compose exec php bin/sightpress system:check --site=demo --recommend

    It prints lines ready to copy into .env, or into the settings of PHP, nginx, Apache or Caddy. Leave out --site=demo to get the values that suit all your websites.

  4. If the values differ from yours, change them and restart, as in Fix upload size limits.

To go back to the installation's limits:

docker compose exec php bin/sightpress site:media:limits demo --reset

items.title: Check what the web server really accepts
items.text:
SightPress can't read the web server's limit, so it can test it by sending empty files of growing sizes. Nothing is stored. In the standard Docker setup:

docker compose exec php bin/sightpress system:check --probe-url=http://nginx

You should see a line such as Probe: the web server accepts 65 MB and refuses 66 MB. If that is less than SightPress was told, the command says which setting to correct.

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: "The audio limit of 600 MB is above the most this install allows" Raise max in config/tenant.php (step 1), or choose a lower value. The new limit doesn't show on the upload form The server's limit is probably lower. Run the command in step 3 and change the values it prints. "The probe got the answer 404" The address doesn't reach this SightPress. In Docker, use http://nginx and run the command with docker compose exec php.

items.title: Codes we send you
items.text:
A SightPress website never sends you a link to click. When it needs to check that an e-mail address is yours, it sends a 6-digit code instead, and you type that code on the website yourself.

This keeps you safe from fake messages. If you ever get a message that claims to come from a SightPress website and asks you to click a link, it is not from us. Don't click it.

items.title: When you get a code
items.text:
You get a code by e-mail when:

  • you forgot your password and asked for a new one: the code works for 15 minutes;
  • someone invited you to help with a website: the invitation code works for 7 days.

The person who sets up a new website gets a setup code from the command line tool, not by e-mail. They pass it on to the website's first admin, who uses it to choose a password. A setup code works for 7 days.

Each code works only once.

items.title: What a code message looks like
items.text:
• The subject names the website, for example "Your code to reset your password for Riverside Library" or "Ada invited you to Riverside Library". The code itself is never in the subject.
  • The message has the code on its own line, for example 123 456.
  • The message has no links, no web addresses and no pictures.
  • It ends with: "We will never send you a link. Type this code on the page where you asked for it. Never share it with anyone."

items.title: Type a code
items.text:
1. Go to the page that asked for the code. For a password, that is the page you are already on. For an invitation, go to the website's sign-in page and choose Accept an invitation.
  2. Find the field called 6-digit code.
  3. Type the 6 digits. You can type them with or without the space in the middle.
  4. Choose Continue. The page never sends the code by itself, so take your time.
  5. You should see the next step, for example a page where you choose your password.

items.title: If the code doesn't work
items.text:
• Check the digits and try again. After 5 wrong tries the code stops working.
  • A code also stops working when it is too old, when it has been used, or when you asked for a newer one.
  • On the password page, choose Send a new code. You can ask for a new code once a minute; if it is too soon, the page tells you how many seconds to wait.
  • For an invitation, ask the person who invited you to invite you again.
  • For a setup code, ask the person who set up the website for a new one.

items.title: Try it on your computer
items.text: When SightPress runs on your computer, the e-mails with codes go to the test inbox. See Open the test e-mail inbox.

items.title: Create a website
items.text:
One SightPress installation can run many websites. Each website has its own pages, people, files and settings, kept in its own database. This guide shows you how to create a website with the command line tool, and what each part of the command means.

Before you start, follow Getting started up to step 6, so that SightPress runs and has a secret key.

items.title: Create the website, answering questions
items.text:
The easiest way is to let the command ask you everything, one question at a time.

  1. Open a terminal and go to the skeleton folder.

  2. Type:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create

  3. Answer each question and press Enter. Each question says what to type. When it ends with "Press Enter for" and a value, pressing Enter without typing takes that value. When it lists choices, such as "Type person or organization", type one of them; capital letters don't matter.

  4. For the database, the command first asks which engine to use. Press Enter for SQLite: it keeps the website in one file and needs nothing else. Press Enter again to keep the file in the sites folder. If you choose MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL instead, the command asks for the server, port, database name, user name and password one by one, each with a usual value you can keep with Enter. The password isn't shown as you type it, and you type it twice so a typing mistake is caught.
  5. For the main language, type a code such as en-GB or pt-BR. Capital letters don't matter and you can use _ instead of -. The command says the language in words, for example "That is Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR). Is that right?". Type yes or press Enter if it is, or no to type it again.
  6. If an answer isn't right, for example an e-mail address without the part after @, the command says what is wrong and asks again. After 3 wrong answers in a row it stops and creates nothing; just start again.
  7. At the end, the command lists all your answers, one per line, and asks "Is all of this right?". Press Enter to create the website. Type no to go through the questions again: your answers are kept, so press Enter for each one that was right and type only what you want to change.
  8. You should see one sentence for each thing SightPress did, ending with: The site "demo" is ready at https://localhost. On your own computer, the address to open is http://localhost:8080: answer http://localhost:8080 to the question "Address the site is opened at".
  9. One of the sentences gives the setup code for the first admin, for example: "Give the setup code 388 641 to ada@example.org." Give the code to that person in a way you trust, such as in person or by phone. SightPress doesn't e-mail it.
  10. The first admin goes to the address in that sentence (for example http://localhost:8080/login/setup), types their e-mail address and the code, and chooses a password. Step 8 of Getting started shows each screen.

items.title: Create the website with one command
items.text:
If you already know every answer, for example in a script, give them all on one line. The command then asks nothing. This example creates a website called "Riverside Library" for an organisation:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create demo --domain=localhost --db-engine=sqlite --url=http://localhost:8080 --owner-type=organization --locale=en-GB --name="Riverside Library" --admin-email=ada@example.org --admin-first-name=Ada --admin-last-name=Lovelace

If something is wrong, the command says what, and creates nothing.

items.title: What each part means
items.text:
Part What to give Example demo A short name for the website: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. You use it in other commands. library --domain The web addresses of the website, without https://, separated by commas. Each address belongs to one website only. On your own computer, use localhost. library.example.org,www.library.example.org --db-engine The database engine: sqlite, mysql, mariadb or postgresql. On your own computer, SQLite is simplest. See Start a database server for the others. sqlite --db-path For SQLite: the file. Optional: without it, a file named after the short name in the sites folder. library.sqlite --db-host, --db-port, --db-name, --db-user, --db-password For the other engines: the server, its port, the database, and the user name and password. Without them, localhost, the engine's usual port, sightpress_ and the short name, sightpress and no password. --db-host=db --db-user=library --db Instead of the parts above: the whole database address in one go. sqlite:////app/sites/library.sqlite --owner-type Who runs the website: organization or person, in capitals or not. The ready-made pages say "we" for an organisation and "I" for a person. person --locale The website's main language. Capital letters don't matter, and _ works as well as -. en-GB, pt_br, fr-FR --name The name visitors see. Optional: without it, the short name is used. "Riverside Library" --admin-email, --admin-first-name, --admin-last-name The first admin of the website. ada@example.org --timezone Optional. The time zone for dates on the website. Europe/London --url Optional. The address printed with the setup code. Without it, SightPress prints https:// and the first domain. On your own computer, use http://localhost:8080. http://localhost:8080 --create-db Optional. Creates the database on a MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL server if it doesn't exist yet. --with-demo-content Optional. Adds demo pages, files and people for trying SightPress out. Don't use it for a real website.

Put quotation marks around anything with spaces, such as the website's name.

items.title: What a new website has
items.text:
Every new website starts ready to use:

  • six published pages: a home page called "Welcome to" and the website's name, About, Contact (with a contact form whose messages go to the first admin), a privacy notice, terms of use and an accessibility statement;
  • a main menu with About and Contact, and a footer menu with the other three pages;
  • a logo, an icon and a picture for sharing on social media, made from the website's name;
  • the roles admin, editor, contributor and member (see Roles and permissions).

The ready-made pages are in English, whatever the website's language. Change or translate them in the admin panel.

items.title: Try SightPress with demo content
items.text:
Add --with-demo-content to the command to fill the new website with examples:

  • five files in the media library: a picture, a short video with captions, a sound recording and a PDF;
  • a page called "Every kind of block" at /every-block, with one block of every kind, and a page under it;
  • three more people, each waiting for their setup code: Bea Okafor (editor), Cleo Martins (contributor) and Max Müller (member).

The command prints a setup code for each person. The example.org addresses can't receive e-mail, so give the codes to whoever tries the website out.

items.title: Give someone a new setup code
items.text:
A setup code works once, for 7 days. To make a new one for an admin who hasn't chosen a password yet, type:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:user:create-admin demo --email=ada@example.org --first-name=Ada --last-name=Lovelace --url=http://localhost:8080

You should see a new setup code. The old one stops working. The same command adds another admin when you give a new e-mail address. Someone who already has a password uses Forgot your password? on the sign-in page instead.

items.title: Turn a website off, or remove it
items.text:
To Type Visitors see turn it off for a while bin/sightpress site:disable demo "temporarily unavailable" turn it on again bin/sightpress site:enable demo the website close it and keep its data bin/sightpress site:archive demo "gone" delete it, softly bin/sightpress site:delete demo "not found"; the data is kept remove a deleted website for good bin/sightpress site:purge demo —

Start each command with docker compose run --rm --no-deps php, as above. site:purge keeps the database unless you add --drop-database, which can't be undone. The command line reference lists every command.

items.title: Fix upload size limits
items.text: How large a file you can upload depends on two things: what the website accepts for each kind of file, and what the server accepts in one go. This guide explains the warning admins see when the server's settings are too low, and how to change them.

items.title: What you see
items.text:
• Next to the upload field in Media, everyone sees the largest file they can upload, for example "Largest file you can upload: pictures 20 MB, documents 50 MB, audio files 200 MB and videos 1 GB." Large files are sent in parts. Without JavaScript the lower server limit applies, and the hint says so.
  • If you choose a file that is too large, the browser refuses it before sending it. The reason appears under the field, which gets focus, so screen readers read it out.
  • If something too large is sent anyway, you see a page called This is too large to send. It says how much the server accepts and has a Go back to the form link.
  • Admins see a warning called Your server’s settings stop some uploads on the dashboard and in Media. Each point names a server setting and the value it needs. It also says how many uploads the web server refused in the last 7 days. Editors and contributors don't see it.
  • To put the warning away, choose Hide until this changes. It comes back by itself if the result changes.

items.title: Change the limits on your own computer
items.text:
With SightPress running in Docker, the limits are one group of lines in the .env file of the skeleton folder. PHP and the web server both read them, so they always match.

  1. If there is no .env file in the skeleton folder yet, create it by copying the example:

    cp .env.example .env

  2. Open .env in a text editor and find the lines that start with UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE.

  3. Change the values you need:

    Setting Recommended What it is UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE 64M The largest file in one upload INPUT_MAX_SIZE 8M The largest form without files, such as a long page INPUT_MAX_VARS 5000 How many fields one form can have; lower values can lose content MAX_FILE_UPLOADS 20 How many files one upload can hold PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT 256M Memory for one request; 512M for pictures over 25 million pixels UPLOAD_TIMEOUT 300 Seconds a slow upload may take

    Sizes are whole megabytes or gigabytes, such as 64M or 1G. On a small site or shared hosting, 32M is enough for UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE.

  4. Save the file and restart SightPress:

    docker compose up -d

  5. Check the result:

    docker compose exec php bin/sightpress system:check

    You should see the limits, the largest file of each kind, and No problems found. If something is still wrong, it is listed with the setting to change.

If a value is not valid, for example UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE=lots, SightPress doesn't start and the terminal says which value to fix.

items.title: On a hosting provider's server
items.text: If someone else runs your server, send them the warning's text. It names the settings, for example upload_max_filesize, post_max_size or the web server's limit (client_max_body_size for nginx), and the value each needs. Ask them to tell you when it is done, then open the dashboard again: the warning is gone once the settings are right.

items.title: Choose how large each website's files can be
items.text: To give one website larger or smaller limits than the others, see Choose upload limits.

items.title: Large audio files and videos
items.text: The website accepts audio files up to 200 MB and videos up to 1 GB. With JavaScript, SightPress sends large files in parts, so they can be larger than UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE. Without JavaScript, one upload can't be larger than UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE. system:check mentions this lower limit as a note, not a problem.

items.title: Import files from a folder
items.text:
If you have many files, or files too large for the browser, you can add them to a website's media library from the server. This is done by whoever runs your SightPress installation. Website limits on file size don't apply, but every safety check does.

Start each command with docker compose run --rm --no-deps php, as in Try the command line tool. The folder must be one the command can read: with Docker, put it inside the skeleton folder.

  1. Import a folder into the website demo, including the folders inside it:

    bin/sightpress site:media:import demo imports/ --recursive

  2. Read the result. Each file gets a line, then a summary such as Imported: 12. Already present: 1. Refused: 1.

  3. Open Media in the admin panel. New files are unpublished until you describe and publish them.

items.title: Options
items.text: Option What it does --recursive Also imports the files inside folders. --publish Publishes the new files straight away. --alt="…" Gives every new picture this description. Use it only if it is true of all of them. --locale=pt-PT The language of that description. The default is the website's main language. --memory-limit=2G Gives this run more memory, for very large pictures.

items.title: What happens to each file
items.text:
• Imported: the file passed the checks and is in the library.
  • Already present: the library already has exactly this file, so it isn't stored twice.
  • Refused: the line says why, for example that a file isn't really the type its name says. The import carries on with the other files, and the command ends with an error so that scripts notice.

A very large picture is refused with the memory it needs. Run the command again with --memory-limit= and that value.

items.title: Install and change a theme
items.text:
A theme decides how your websites look: colours, fonts, spacing and the layout of the pages. Every SightPress installation has the default theme, and you can install more. Each website then uses one of the installed themes, and you can change it at any time. Your pages and their content stay the same: only the look changes.

Installing a theme is done by whoever runs your SightPress installation, on the server. Choosing a theme for a website is done by one of its admins.

No theme is installed from the admin panel

For safety, themes are never uploaded through the website. They are installed on the server, the same way as SightPress itself.

items.title: Install a theme
items.text:
You need the name of the theme's package, for example acme/theme-harbour. Run these in your project folder. With Docker, put docker compose run --rm --no-deps php in front of each one, as in Try the command line tool:

  1. Install the package: composer require acme/theme-harbour.
  2. Let SightPress notice it: bin/sightpress cache:clear.
  3. Check it: bin/sightpress theme:validate acme-harbour. You should see "The theme … passes". If it fails, the message says what is wrong, for example a colour pair that is too hard to read, with the colours and the ratio. A theme that fails can't be used until its author fixes it.
  4. See every theme: bin/sightpress theme:list. Each line shows the theme, its version, whether websites may use it, and which websites use it.

items.title: Choose which themes websites may use
items.text:
By default, every installed theme can be used by every website, and new websites start with the default theme. To change that, edit config/tenant.php:

'themes' => [
    // Only these themes can be chosen; null means every installed theme.
    'allowed' => ['default', 'acme-harbour'],
    // The theme of new websites. It must be one of the allowed themes.
    'default' => 'acme-harbour',
],

If the default theme isn't one of the allowed themes, SightPress won't start and says why.

items.title: Change the theme of a website
items.text:
In the admin panel (you need to be an admin of the website):

  1. In the admin menu, choose Appearance.
  2. You should see one section for each installed theme, with its name as a heading, what it is like, and its Status in words, for example "The site's theme" or "Available". If a picture of the theme was made, it is there with a description; otherwise the description is written out.
  3. To look first, choose Preview … (it opens in a new tab): a sample page with every kind of block in that theme.
  4. Choose Use …. If some pages use a layout the theme doesn't have, a page lists them first: they will be shown in the standard layout, and they keep their own layout for later. Choose Use … again to go ahead, or Keep the current theme.
  5. A message at the top says the theme is now the site's theme. Screen readers read the message out.

Or from the command line: bin/sightpress site:theme:apply demo acme-harbour (the website's short name, then the theme). SightPress checks the theme again before it applies it, and the website's activity log records the change.

Open the website: it now has the new look. The other websites keep theirs.

items.title: Change the colours of the theme
items.text:
1. On the Appearance screen, choose Change the colours of the site's theme.
  2. You should see two groups, Light mode and Dark mode, each with the background, text, links, buttons and highlights, text on buttons, borders and the focus outline. Each colour is written as # and six digits or letters, for example #0a57c2.
  3. Change a colour and choose Save the colours.
  4. If the colour is too hard to read against the colours next to it, SightPress refuses it and says which colours clash and by how much, for example "on-primary on primary has a contrast of 2.14:1 in light mode; it needs at least 4.5:1". What you typed is kept, so you can adjust it.
  5. To undo your changes, choose Use the theme's own colours.

The admin panel keeps its own colours whatever you choose.

items.title: Choose a layout for each page
items.text: Themes offer layouts such as Landing, Sidebar and Full width. See Choose a page layout.

items.title: Pictures of each theme
items.text: The pictures and previews on the Appearance screen are made on the server by bin/sightpress theme:publish-assets, which runs after every composer install and composer update. Pictures need Node.js and the Chromium browser on the server; without them, the screen describes each theme in words and still links to its preview.

items.title: Remove a theme
items.text:
1. Run bin/sightpress theme:list to see which websites use the theme.
  2. Give those websites another theme first (see above).
  3. Remove the package: composer remove acme/theme-harbour, then bin/sightpress cache:clear.

If a website still used the theme, nothing breaks: the website is shown in the default theme. Its admins see "Your site is shown in the default theme" on the dashboard, with the reason, and the server log notes it too. Choosing a theme for the website again makes the message go away.

items.title: The admin panel keeps its look
items.text: The admin panel always uses the look of the default theme, whatever theme a website has. Admins can always find their way around, and the admin panel keeps its contrast.

items.title: Keep your files in the cloud
items.text:
By default, a website keeps its pictures, videos and other files on your server. You can move them to cloud storage instead, and let a CDN (content delivery network) deliver public files from near each visitor. Both are optional. Nothing is sent to another company unless you set it up.

This is done by whoever runs your SightPress installation, with the command line tool. Start each command with docker compose run --rm --no-deps php, as in Try the command line tool. The examples use a website called demo.

Before you start

  • It may cost money. AWS and Cloudflare charge for storage and traffic. Check their prices first.
  • Your files move to another company. Files can contain personal data, so say so in your privacy notice. If the location is outside your country, that may be an international transfer of personal data.
  • Keep a copy of the sites folder until you have checked the website.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Which service to use
items.text:
SightPress works with any S3-compatible service, such as AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces or MinIO.

SightPress can create what you need at AWS or Cloudflare. For another service, create a private bucket in its control panel and go to Connect the bucket.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Create the bucket and CDN
items.text:
1. Put your provider's keys in the environment for this one run. SightPress never saves them.
    • AWS: SIGHTPRESS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and SIGHTPRESS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY.
    • Cloudflare: SIGHTPRESS_CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID and SIGHTPRESS_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. To use your own domain with --domain, also set SIGHTPRESS_CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID.

  2. Read the plan. This contacts nobody and changes nothing:

    bin/sightpress site:storage:provision demo --provider=aws --dry-run

    You should see each item that will be created and its location. 3. Run the same command without --dry-run to create them. It is safe to run it twice.

What is created. At AWS: a private bucket, a CloudFront CDN that alone can read it, permission for browsers to upload to it from your website, and rules that clear unfinished uploads. At Cloudflare: an R2 bucket with the same upload permission and rules, and a public address if you use --domain.

Where it is created. The location follows the website's time zone:

Website's time zone AWS Cloudflare R2 United Kingdom London (eu-west-2) EU, because R2 has no UK location EU, EEA or Switzerland Frankfurt (eu-central-1) EU Anywhere else You choose with --region You choose with --region (eu, us or default)

Creating these doesn't change your website yet.

To let the website's admins do this under Site settings, then File storage, set SIGHTPRESS_PROVISION_FROM_ADMIN=1 and the provider's keys in the web server's environment. They can then create things that cost money in that account, so only do this if you trust them with it.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Connect the bucket
items.text:
1. Create keys limited to this bucket in your provider's control panel, and set them as SIGHTPRESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY and SIGHTPRESS_S3_SECRET_KEY. SightPress stores them encrypted.

  2. Connect the bucket. For a provider other than AWS, add its address with --endpoint. MinIO also needs --path-style.

    bin/sightpress site:storage:s3 demo --bucket=my-bucket --region=eu-west-2

    You should see that the bucket works and has been saved. The website still uses its local files.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Move the files
items.text:
bin/sightpress site:storage:migrate demo

SightPress copies each file, checks it arrived intact, and then switches the website. If it stops, run it again and it goes on from where it was. Your local copies stay until you are sure. To delete them after the check, run the command again with --delete-source. This can't be undone.

Open the website and check that its pictures and files appear.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Turn on the CDN
items.text:
1. Set the CDN to fetch from your website, forward its host name, include the query string in its cache key, and not forward cookies.

  2. Turn it on, with an address that starts with https://, and publish the theme's files:

    bin/sightpress site:storage:cdn demo --url=https://cdn.example.org
bin/sightpress theme:publish-assets

To stop using it, run bin/sightpress site:storage:cdn demo --remove.

Private files stay protected. Unpublished files and every file of a members-only website use signed addresses that stop working after a short time. After you unpublish a file or make a website members-only, a copy on the CDN can last up to five minutes.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Check it
items.text: Website admins can see where files are kept under Site settings, then File storage: the provider, the bucket, the region and the CDN address. Keys are never shown.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: The command says the bucket can't be reached or the keys are wrong Nothing was changed. Check the bucket name, the region, the address and the keys, then run it again. Large uploads say they're using the server instead The bucket doesn't allow uploads from your website's address. Files still upload, through your server. Add your website's address to the bucket's CORS rules, allowing PUT and exposing ETag. A website is deleted site:purge also removes that website's folder in the bucket.
path: Keep your files in the cloud

items.title: Let people sign up
items.text:
By default only people you invite can have an account on your website. You can also let anyone create their own account. They confirm their email address with a 6-digit code before they can sign in.

You need to be an admin.

items.title: Turn sign-up on
items.text:
1. Choose Site settings in the admin menu, then Change who can sign up.
  2. Tick Let anyone create an account.
  3. In Role of people who sign up, keep Member unless you have a reason to change it. Members can read members-only pages and nothing more. Only roles that are safe to give to people you don't know are listed: never editor or admin.
  4. Choose Save sign-up settings. You should see "The sign-up settings have been saved."

The sign-in page now shows "New here?" with a Create an account link.

items.title: Try it as a new person
items.text:
1. Sign out, or open a private browser window, and go to the sign-in page, for example http://localhost:8080/login.
  2. Choose Create an account. Fill in your first name, last name, an optional display name, your email address, your time zone (your browser's is already chosen) and a password. On a website in several languages, choose your language too.
  3. Choose Create my account. You should see the heading Confirm your email address.
  4. Open the email. While you try SightPress on your computer, it is in the test inbox: see Open the test e-mail inbox. It has a 6-digit code and no link.
  5. Type the code in 6-digit code and choose Confirm my email address. You should see "Your email address is confirmed and your account is ready."
  6. Sign in with your email address and password.

The code works once, for 15 minutes. Send a new code sends another one, at most once a minute. See Codes we send you.

items.title: What keeps it safe
items.text:
• An account can't sign in until its email address is confirmed. Accounts that are never confirmed are removed after a week.
  • If someone signs up with an address that already has an account, the page looks exactly the same, so nobody can find out who has an account. The owner of the address gets an email saying someone tried, with no link.
  • A hidden field catches most automated sign-ups, and each place can send at most 10 sign-up forms an hour. There are no picture puzzles.
  • Every new account and every change to these settings is written to the Audit log.

To turn sign-up off again, untick Let anyone create an account. Accounts that were already made are kept.

items.title: Make a website or a page members-only
items.text:
A members-only page can only be read by people who have an account on the website and are signed in. You can make a single page members-only, or the whole website.

You need to be an admin to change the whole website, and an editor or admin to change a page.

items.title: Make one page members-only
items.text:
1. Choose Pages in the admin menu, then the page.
  2. In About the page, under Who can read this page, choose Members only: people with an account on the site, once they sign in.
  3. Choose Save page.
  4. Check: sign out, or open a private browser window, and go to the page. You should see the sign-in page. After signing in, you are taken back to the page.

A members-only page is left out of search engines, the sitemap, llms.txt and site search for visitors who aren't signed in. In the menus, it only appears for people who are signed in.

To show a menu entry only to members, for example a link to a members' forum, choose Menus, then Change next to the entry, and tick Only show this entry to members who are signed in.

items.title: Make the whole website members-only
items.text:
1. Choose Site settings in the admin menu.
  2. Under Who can read the site, choose Only people with an account, once they sign in. Search engines and AI services can’t read any page.
  3. Choose Save settings. You should see "The settings have been saved."
  4. Check: in a private browser window, go to any page of the website. You should see the sign-in page with the message "This site is for its members. Sign in to read it."

On a members-only website:

  • People who aren't signed in can still sign in, create an account (if you let them, see Let people sign up), reset a forgotten password and accept an invitation.
  • Search engines and AI services can't read anything: the sitemap and llms.txt are empty, and every page asks not to be listed.
  • Every signed-in person, whatever their role, can read every published page.

items.title: Who can read what
items.text:
Visitors who aren't signed in Members (signed in) Editors and admins Pages for everyone, on a public website Yes Yes Yes Members-only pages No: asked to sign in Yes Yes Any page of a members-only website No: asked to sign in Yes Yes Drafts, older versions, archived pages No No Yes The admin panel No No Yes

To give people accounts, invite them from Invite someone in the admin menu, or let them sign up themselves.

items.title: Move or rename a page without breaking links
items.text:
When a published page gets a new address, or moves somewhere else on the website, SightPress remembers its old address. Anyone who follows an old link or bookmark is taken to the new address, and search engines are told that the page has moved for good. You don't need to do anything for this to happen.

You need to be an editor or admin.

items.title: Give a page a new address
items.text:
1. Choose Pages in the admin menu, then the page.
  2. In Address, type the new last part of the address, for example opening-times instead of hours. Use lower-case letters, digits and hyphens.
  3. Choose Save page.
  4. Check: open the old address, for example http://localhost:8080/hours. You should land on http://localhost:8080/opening-times.

Pages under it move with it: /hours/holidays becomes /opening-times/holidays, and its old address leads there too.

items.title: Move a page somewhere else on the website
items.text:
In the page editor, the Place in the site section has these buttons:

  • Move up and Move down change the order of pages at the same level, for example in a menu of pages.
  • Move under the page before it puts the page one level down, under the page just above it.
  • Move out to the level above puts the page one level up.
  • Move to: choose The top level of the site or any other page in the list, then choose Move the page.

After each move, a message says where the page is now, and focus stays in the section. Pages under it move with it, and every old address leads to the new one.

items.title: See and change the redirects
items.text:
1. Choose Redirects in the admin menu. You should see the table Old addresses and where they lead, with each Old address, its Language and where it Leads to. A page that was deleted for good shows "Gone: the page was deleted".
  2. To stop an old address leading anywhere, choose Remove the redirect from followed by that address.
  3. To add your own, for example for a page from an old website, fill in Old address (such as /old-news) and New address (such as /news) under Add a redirect, then choose Add redirect. The new address must be in the same language.

A few rules keep this tidy:

  • If a page moves twice, its oldest address leads straight to the newest one, never through a chain.
  • A redirect that would go round in a circle is refused.
  • A new page that uses an old address wins: the redirect stops and visitors see the new page.

The Pages not found report on the Analytics screen lists addresses people asked for that don't exist, with a link to add a redirect for each. See See who visits your website.

items.title: Open the file storage console
items.text:
SightPress comes with a file storage program called MinIO, which has its own web console. This guide shows you how to sign in to it.

  1. Start SightPress (see Getting started).
  2. In your web browser, go to http://localhost:9001.
  3. You should see the MinIO sign-in page.
  4. Sign in with the user name sightpress and the password sightpress-secret.
  5. You should see the MinIO console. There are no files yet.

By default, each website keeps its uploaded files, such as pictures and documents, in its own folder inside the sites folder of the skeleton, so MinIO stays empty. The site:storage:s3 command can move a website's storage to MinIO or another S3-compatible service.

If you changed MINIO_ROOT_USER, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD or MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT in your .env file, use your values instead. These settings only take effect the first time the storage starts.

items.title: Open the test e-mail inbox
items.text:
When SightPress runs on your computer, it never sends real e-mail. Every message goes to a test inbox called Mailpit instead, so you can read it without anything leaving your computer. This guide shows you how to open it.

  1. Start SightPress (see Getting started).
  2. In your web browser, go to http://localhost:8025.
  3. You should see the Mailpit inbox. It is empty for now, with a message saying there are no messages.

SightPress sends e-mail when:

  • someone forgets their password and asks for a code;
  • someone is invited to help with a website;
  • a page is sent for review: every editor and admin is told;
  • a visitor sends a message with a contact form.

Each of these messages appears here a moment later. Choose a message to read it.

The inbox only gets messages when your .env file has the line MAILER_DSN=smtp://mailpit:1025. The file you copied from .env.example in Getting started already has it. Without it, SightPress sends nothing.

If you changed MAILPIT_UI_PORT in your .env file, use that number instead of 8025.

items.title: Plan your website
items.text:
This guide helps you decide how to set up a SightPress website before you build it. Answer a few questions about what the website needs. The guide then suggests the settings to choose and the content to write.

You don't need to be technical to do the planning. Some choices are made by whoever runs your SightPress installation, and this guide says which ones.

Which version this guide describes

This guide describes version 0.4. If you run 0.3, update first: it has no cloud storage, other themes, extra page layouts or per-website upload limits. See Update SightPress.

items.title: Step 1: Answer these questions
items.text:
Write down your answers. Each one points to a choice in the next steps.

Question Why it matters Who is the website for, and what must they be able to do? Decides your pages and calls to action. Is it public, or only for members? Decides who can read it and whether search engines can find it. Who will write, check and publish pages? Decides the roles you give people. Which languages do you need?
