            [--name=] [--timezone=] [--url=] [--create-db] [--with-demo-content] [--without=]

Creates a website: its database tables, its roles, its first admin, six starter pages, its menus and its logo, icon and share image. It prints the first admin's setup code. Nothing is created if something is wrong. Create a website explains every option. --without= names optional features (module ids, separated by commas) the website starts with off.

items.title: site:user:create-admin
items.text:
site:user:create-admin <slug> --email= --first-name= --last-name= [--url=]

Creates an admin on a website and prints the setup code they choose their password with. For an admin who hasn't chosen a password yet, it prints a new code, and the old one stops working. Someone who can already sign in is refused: they use "Forgot your password?" instead.

items.title: Turn websites on and off
items.text:
Command What it does Visitors see site:enable <slug> Turns a website on, so it answers again. Also brings back a deleted website. the website site:disable <slug> Turns a website off for a while. "temporarily unavailable" (503) site:archive <slug> Archives a website. Its data is kept. "gone" (410) site:delete <slug> Deletes a website, softly: it stops answering and its data is kept until site:purge. "not found" (404) site:purge <slug> [--drop-database] Removes a deleted website for good. Its database is kept unless you add --drop-database, which can't be undone. —

Every change is written to the installation's log.

items.title: Look after websites
items.text:
Command What it does site:list Lists the websites: status, domains, language, time zone and database (engine, host and name only). site:migrate <slug> or site:migrate --all Updates a website's database tables after an update of SightPress. --all updates every website that isn't deleted; one failure doesn't stop the others. site:db:change <slug> [--db= or the --db-… parts] [--migrate] Points a disabled website at another database, asked for in parts like in site:create. Nothing is copied: move the data first. The new database must be up to date, or add --migrate. If anything fails, the website keeps its old database. site:seo:check <slug> Checks what search engines will find: titles longer than 60 characters, missing or too long descriptions, pages left out of search and why. Ends with an error when two pages have the same title. See Search and AI visibility.

| system:check [--site=<slug>] [--probe-url=<address>] [--recommend] | Lists the server's upload and input limits, the largest file of each kind that can be uploaded, and the settings to change. Ends with an error when something must be fixed. --site checks one website's limits and counts the uploads refused for it. --probe-url sends test requests to find the web server's real limit. --recommend prints the server values the limits need. Run it with docker compose exec php so it reads the same settings as the website. See Choose upload limits. | | site:media:limits <slug> [--image=] [--video=] [--audio=] [--document=] [--pixels=] [--reset] | Shows or changes the largest files a website accepts, up to the most the installation allows. See Choose upload limits. |

To move a website to another database:

bin/sightpress site:disable demo
# copy the data to the new database with your database's own tools
bin/sightpress site:db:change demo --db=postgresql://user:password@db.internal:5432/demo
bin/sightpress site:enable demo

items.title: Languages
items.text:
Command What it does site:locale:add <slug> <locale> Adds a language to the website, for example site:locale:add demo pt-PT. Pages are then translated into it from each page's editor. site:locale:default <slug> <locale> Makes one of the website's languages the main one, whose pages have addresses without a language part. Warns that addresses change. site:locale:remove <slug> <locale> [--yes] Removes a language. Without --yes it only explains what would happen. Its translations are kept, unreachable, and come back if the language is added again. The main language can't be removed.

See Add a language and translate a page.

items.title: Things that happen at a set time
schedule:run
items.text:
schedule:run

Does everything that is due on every website that is on: publishes and unpublishes scheduled pages, rolls up and deletes old analytics, rebuilds search indexes that are out of date and removes sign-ups that were never confirmed. It prints a line for each thing it did and a summary. Run it once a minute: the skeleton's scheduler service does this in Docker; on a server, add a crontab line (see Update SightPress). Two runs never overlap: the second says "Another run is still going; this one stops." A missed run catches up on the next one. See Schedule a page.

items.title: Features
items.text:
Command What it does site:module:list <slug> Lists the website's optional features (modules): id, name and whether each one is on. site:module:enable <slug> <module> Turns a feature on, after updating the website's database for it. Refused while a feature it needs is off. site:module:disable <slug> <module> [--purge-data] Turns a feature off; its data is kept. Refused while a feature that is on needs it. --purge-data also deletes its data, for good.

Features the installation set in config/tenant.php (modules.locked) can't be changed. See Turn features on or off.

items.title: Site search
items.text:
Command What it does site:search:reindex <slug> [--locale=<locale>] Builds the website's search index again from its published pages, in every language or one. site:search:status <slug> How many pages the search index holds in each language, when it last changed, and whether it is waiting to be rebuilt. site:search <slug> <words> [--locale=<locale>] [--members] Searches the website the way a visitor would (--members: as someone signed in) and lists the first results.

They refuse a website with search turned off. See Search your website.

items.title: Analytics
items.text:
Command What it does site:analytics:report <slug> [--from=YYYY-MM-DD] [--to=YYYY-MM-DD] [--report=<name>\|all] [--format=table\|csv\|json] Shows the website's analytics, the last 30 days by default. Reports: summary, daily, pages, sources, languages, devices, searches, searches-without-results, not-found, bots. Warns when the hourly roll-up hasn't run for two hours. site:analytics:purge <slug> [--before=YYYY-MM-DD] Deletes the figures from before a day; without --before, those older than the website keeps them.

They refuse a website with analytics turned off. See See who visits your website.

items.title: AI assistant
items.text:
Command What it does site:assistant:set <slug> --provider=<id> --model=<model> [--base-url=<address>] [--key-stdin] Chooses the AI service (anthropic, openai, mistral or openai_compatible) and model. With --key-stdin it reads the API key from standard input, so it never appears in the shell history: printf %s "$KEY" \| bin/sightpress site:assistant:set …. site:assistant:test <slug> Sends a tiny request and says whether the service answered. site:assistant:usage <slug> [--month=YYYY-MM] Shows the tokens used this month (or another), per task, and the budget. site:assistant:disable <slug> [--remove-key] Turns the assistant off for the website, and removes its key with --remove-key. assistant:ask <slug> "<question>" Asks the assistant a question from the console.

They refuse a website with the assistant turned off; turn it on with site:module:enable <slug> assistant. See Use the AI assistant.

items.title: Branding
items.text:
Command What it does site:branding:set <slug> [--logo=] [--logo-alt=] [--icon=] [--share-image=] [--share-image-alt=] Uses picture files for the logo (SVG, PNG, JPEG or WebP, from 1:1 to 8:1 wide), the icon (a square PNG, JPEG or WebP of at least 512 × 512 pixels) or the share image (PNG, JPEG or WebP of 1200 × 630 pixels, or larger with the same proportions). The -alt options say what the picture shows, for screen readers; the default is the website's name. site:branding:reset <slug> [--logo] [--icon] [--share-image] Goes back to the generated logo, icon or share image; all three unless you name some. site:branding:regenerate <slug> Makes the generated pictures again from the website's name, for example after renaming it. Uploaded pictures stay.

Admins can do the same in the admin panel, under Branding.

items.title: The site registry
items.text:
The installation keeps its list of websites in config/sites.php, with each database address encrypted with APP_SECRET.

Command What it does site:registry:check Checks the file, and that every database address can be read with this APP_SECRET, and says what to fix. site:registry:upgrade Upgrades the file to the format this version of SightPress reads.

Each change to the file keeps the previous version as config/sites.php.bak.

items.title: Files and cloud storage
items.text:
See Keep your files in the cloud and Import files from a folder.

Command What it does site:storage:provision <slug> --provider=aws\|cloudflare [--region=] [--bucket=] [--domain=] [--dry-run] Creates a bucket, its upload rules and a CDN at AWS or Cloudflare. --dry-run prints the plan and contacts nobody. The provider's keys come from the environment and are never saved. The website doesn't change. site:storage:s3 <slug> --bucket= --region= [--endpoint=] [--prefix=] [--path-style] Connects a website to an S3-compatible bucket after checking it works. The keys come from SIGHTPRESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY and SIGHTPRESS_S3_SECRET_KEY, and are stored encrypted. site:storage:migrate <slug> [--delete-source] Copies a website's files to its bucket, checks each one and switches the website. It can be run again if it stops. --delete-source deletes the local copies after the check, which can't be undone. site:storage:cdn <slug> [--url=] [--remove] Shows, sets or removes the https:// CDN address that delivers a website's public files. Run theme:publish-assets after setting it. site:media:import <slug> <path>… [--recursive] [--publish] [--alt=] [--locale=] [--memory-limit=] Adds files of any size from the server to the media library, with every safety check. Ends with an error if any file was refused, after trying the others. site:media:uploads <slug> [--purge-expired] Lists uploads in progress. --purge-expired removes those idle for 24 hours and the records of those finished 7 days ago. The scheduler also does this.

items.title: Themes
items.text: See Install and change a theme.

items.title: theme:list
items.text:
theme:list

Lists the installed themes: id, name, version, whether websites may use it (or why it can't be used), whether new websites start with it, and the websites that use it. Websites whose theme isn't installed any more are listed as errors; they are shown in the default theme.

items.title: theme:validate
items.text:
theme:validate [<theme>|<path>] [--axe]

Checks a theme the way it is checked before it is applied, and says what to fix:

  • theme.json and the theme's manifest agree;
  • the colour contrast passes in light and dark mode, with and without more contrast, chart colours included, against WCAG 2.2 AA, and the base font size is at least 16 px;
  • the required templates are there, and the page shell includes SightPress's <head> partial;
  • the theme ships no screenshot or preview output.

Give an installed theme's id or the folder of a theme. Without one, it checks every installed theme. --axe also scans the theme's preview page with axe in light, dark and forced-colours mode; this needs Node.js and Playwright's Chromium. It ends with an error when a check fails.

items.title: theme:preview
items.text:
theme:preview <theme|path> [--out=build/theme-preview/<id>] [--locale=en-GB] [--screenshot]

Writes the theme's preview page to a folder that opens in any browser without a server or an internet connection: a top bar, a band with the theme's name and a Download button, one block of every kind, and the footer. --screenshot also writes screenshot.png, screenshot-dark.png and page.png (needs Node.js and Playwright's Chromium). Theme authors can run the same commands without a project with vendor/bin/sightpress-theme.

items.title: site:theme:apply
items.text:
site:theme:apply <site> <theme>

Applies an installed theme to a website. The theme must be allowed (themes.allowed in config/tenant.php) and pass the checks of theme:validate. The website's activity log records the change.

items.title: theme:publish-assets
items.text:
theme:publish-assets [--no-screenshot]

Writes the preview page of every installed theme to public/themes/<theme>/<version>/preview/, with its screenshots where Node.js and Chromium are installed, for the Appearance screen. The project runs it after composer install and composer update.

items.title: cache:clear
items.text:
cache:clear

Empties the cache folder. Run it after installing or removing a theme or a module with Composer.

items.title: Database addresses
items.text:
--db takes the address (DSN) of a database:

Engine Example SQLite (a file) sqlite:////app/sites/demo.sqlite MySQL mysql://user:password@mysql:3306/demo MariaDB mariadb://user:password@mariadb:3306/demo PostgreSQL postgresql://user:password@postgres:5432/demo

A SQLite file and its folder are created when missing. On the other engines the database must exist, unless you add --create-db to site:create and the database user is allowed to create databases. To start a database server on your computer, see Start a database server.

items.title: Roles and permissions
items.text: Everyone who signs in to a SightPress website has one role. A role is a set of permissions: each permission lets a person do one thing, such as publish pages. Each website keeps its own people and roles, so someone can be an editor on one website and a contributor on another.

items.title: The four roles
items.text:
Every new website has these roles. The admin panel describes each one in the same words when you invite someone or change their role.

Role What the admin panel says In short Admin Can do everything, including inviting people, changing roles and site settings. Runs the website. Editor Can write, review and publish any page, and invite contributors. Looks after the content. Contributor Can write pages and send them for review, but not publish them. Writes. Member Can sign in and read the site, but not use the admin panel. Reads.

The admin and member roles can't be renamed or deleted. The member role never has any permission. Every new website has one admin: the person named when it was created (see Create a website).

items.title: What each role can do
items.text:
Permission What it lets you do Admin Editor Contributor Member Use the admin panel Sign in to the admin panel. yes yes yes no Create pages Start new pages. yes yes yes no Edit own pages Change pages they wrote. yes yes yes no Edit any page Change pages anyone wrote. yes yes no no Submit pages for review Send a page to the editors. yes yes yes no Publish pages Approve, publish and unpublish pages. yes yes no no Archive pages Take pages off the site and keep them. yes yes no no Delete pages Delete pages for good. yes yes no no Upload media Add pictures, video, audio and files. yes yes yes no Publish media Make uploaded files public. yes yes no no Manage menus Change the main and footer menus. yes yes no no Invite people Invite people to the site with a role they are allowed to give. yes yes no no Manage users Change the role of any user, and deactivate accounts. yes no no no Manage roles Create roles and change what they allow. yes no no no Manage site settings Change the site's name, profile, branding and other settings. yes no no no Manage features Turn the site's optional features on and off, and delete their data (how). yes no no no Apply themes Choose the site's theme. yes no no no View the audit log See who changed what, and when. yes no no no View analytics See how many people visit the site, what they read and where they come from (how). yes yes no no Manage analytics Choose how long analytics are kept, and delete them. yes no no no Use the AI assistant Ask the AI assistant for suggestions, which they check before using (how). People who sign up may have it. yes yes yes no Manage the AI assistant Choose the AI service, its key, the monthly budget and who may use the assistant. yes no no no

Archiving pages, deleting pages, more themes and editing roles in the admin panel come in later versions; the permissions already exist so that roles are ready for them.

items.title: Pages and roles
items.text:
Every page goes through the same steps before visitors can see it. Editors' own pages go through review too.

Step From To Who can take it Submit for review Draft Waiting for review The person who wrote the page, or anyone who can edit any page Send back to draft Waiting for review Draft Editors and admins Approve Waiting for review Approved Editors and admins Publish Approved Published Editors and admins Unpublish Published Draft Editors and admins

Only published pages are on the public website. When a page is submitted, every editor and admin (except the person who submitted it) gets an e-mail about it. Contributors see their own pages and published pages in the admin panel, and can't change a page while it waits for review.

items.title: Who can invite whom
items.text:
• Admins can invite someone with any role.
  • Editors can invite contributors only. Their form shows just that role.
  • Contributors and members can't invite anyone.

The invited person gets an e-mail with a 6-digit code, never a link. See Codes we send you.

items.title: Change someone's role
items.text:
Admins do this in the admin panel:

  1. Choose People in the admin menu. You should see a table of everyone with an account.
  2. Choose the person's name.
  3. Under Change role, choose the new role, then choose Change role. You should hear or see, for example, "Cleo’s role is now Editor." The new role applies from the person's next page.

On the same page, Deactivate account stops someone signing in straight away; their pages stay. Reactivate lets them sign in again with their old password. Nobody can change their own role or deactivate themselves, so a website always keeps someone who can manage people.

items.title: For developers
items.text:
Permission names, for modules and the command line: admin.access, page.create, page.edit.own, page.edit.any, page.submit, page.publish, page.archive, page.delete, media.upload, media.publish, menu.manage, user.invite, user.manage, role.manage, settings.manage, module.manage, theme.apply and audit.view.

  • A role that has any permission also has admin.access.
  • A module adds permissions with $registrar->permissions()->add(...). They are copied into every website and given to their default roles, and always to the admin role.
  • The role people get when they register themselves (site setting registration_role, default member) may only hold permissions that are safe for strangers: admin.access, page.create, page.edit.own, page.submit and media.upload. Self-registration arrives in a later version.

items.title: Search and AI visibility
items.text: Every public page of a SightPress website is ready for search engines and for AI search engines and assistants, with nothing to set up. This page explains what SightPress does for each page, and the settings that change it.

items.title: Which pages are shown
items.text:
Search engines and AI readers are only ever offered pages that are:

  • published (drafts and pages waiting for review never are);
  • public;
  • not marked "Ask search engines and AI search engines not to list this page";
  • not a copy of a page on another website (a page with an "Address of the original").

While SightPress runs anywhere other than production (the APP_ENV setting, for example on your own computer), every page asks search engines not to list it, and robots.txt keeps crawlers out of the whole website.

items.title: What every page has
items.text:
• A title: the page's "Title in search results" if it has one, otherwise its title followed by the website's name, such as "About us - Riverside Library".
  • A description: the page's "Description for search engines", otherwise its summary, otherwise its first words. Longer text is cut at a whole word, at 160 characters. Social networks get the same description.
  • One address (the canonical address). An address ending in / moves permanently to the one without it, and the website's other domains move permanently to its first domain.
  • Structured data that search engines read: the page, where it sits in the website, who runs the website (from the site settings) and the pictures, videos and recordings on it.
  • "Last updated" under the content, in the reader's time zone.
  • A Markdown version for AI readers: add .md to the page's address, such as /about.md, or /index.md for the home page. It has the title, the summary, every block as plain text (pictures with their alternative text, videos and recordings with their transcripts, files with their type and size) and the page's address and date. Contact forms are left out.

items.title: Files for search engines and AI readers
items.text:
Address What it is /sitemap.xml Every page search engines may list, in every language, with the date it last changed. /robots.txt Keeps crawlers out of the admin panel, accounts and sign-in pages, points them to the sitemap, and names the AI crawlers the website keeps out. /llms.txt The website's name and summary, then a link to the Markdown version of every page that may be listed, with its description. /llms-full.txt The same pages in full, as Markdown, up to 500 KB. If it stops early, it says how many pages were left out.

The files are made again each time a page is created, saved, moved, published or unpublished.

items.title: Settings
items.text: Admins change these under Site settings, in the Search & AI section.

items.title: AI crawlers
items.text:
Whether AI services may read the public pages, to answer people's questions with a link back (AI search and assistants) and to train their models.

Choice What robots.txt asks Allow all (the default) Nothing extra: every crawler may read the public pages. AI search only Crawlers that train AI models, such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended and CCBot, stay out. AI search and assistants may read the pages and link to them. Block all Every AI crawler stays out: those that train models, and AI search and assistant crawlers such as OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot.

Search engines are never affected. robots.txt is a request that well-behaved crawlers follow, not a lock.

items.title: Search console codes
items.text: To prove to a search engine that the website is yours, it gives you a code. Paste only the code (the part in content="…") into Google Search Console verification code, Bing Webmaster Tools verification code or Yandex Webmaster verification code. SightPress adds it to the home page.

items.title: IndexNow
items.text: Tell search engines at once when a page is published or unpublished (IndexNow) is off by default. When it is on, the website tells the search engines that use IndexNow, such as Bing and Yandex, each time a page is published or unpublished.

items.title: Who runs the site
items.text: The Who runs the site section (a description, full name, contact details and profiles on other websites) goes into the structured data, and the description also goes at the top of llms.txt. Leave a field empty to keep it private.

items.title: Settings on each page
items.text:
In the page editor's Search & AI section:

Field What it does Summary One or two sentences, shown in lists of pages, used as the description when there is none, and read by AI search engines. Title in search results Replaces the title in search results only. Description for search engines Shown under the title in search results. About 160 characters are shown. Picture shown when the page is shared A picture from the media library. Leave it empty to use the website's share image. Shown only when the media library has pictures. Ask search engines and AI search engines not to list this page Keeps the page out of search results, the sitemap, llms.txt and llms-full.txt. Address of the original Only for a copy of a page on another website: its full address. The copy then points search engines to the original, and is left out of the sitemap.

Before publishing, the page's checks suggest a description and a summary when they are missing, and warn about a description longer than 160 characters or a title another page already has.

items.title: Check a website from the command line
items.text:
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:seo:check demo

It lists titles longer than 60 characters, missing or too long descriptions, pages left out of search and why, and whether SightPress runs in production. Two pages with the same title count as a problem, and the command ends with an error.

items.title: Theme contract
items.text:
This page lists what a SightPress theme can rely on and must provide. It is generated from the sightpress/theme-interface package. To build a theme step by step, follow the Create a theme tutorial.

A theme is presentation only: design tokens, Twig templates, assets and translations. Anything with behaviour is a module.

items.title: theme.json
items.text: Key Required What it is name Yes The theme id; must equal the id in the theme's manifest. label Yes Name shown to people. version Yes The theme's version (Semantic Versioning); must equal the version in the theme's manifest. colors Yes The colours for light and dark mode, and optionally for more contrast. typography Yes Fonts and text sizes. spacing No The spacing scale. radius No Corner radii. focus No The focus outline. contrast No Colour pairs core checks in every colour mode: text needs 4.5:1, interface colours 3:1 (WCAG 2.2 AA). chart No Which of the theme's colours the data series of a chart use, in order; without it they use chart-1 to chart-4. Core checks each series colour for 3:1 and chart-text for 4.5:1 on background and surface in every colour mode.

items.title: Token groups
items.text:
Each group becomes CSS custom properties with this prefix.

Group Prefix typography --font- spacing --space- radius --radius- focus --focus-

Charts use the colours chart-1, chart-2, chart-3, chart-4, chart-grid, chart-text.

items.title: Layouts
items.text: Id Name Required What it is default Default Yes One column at a comfortable reading width. home Home Yes An introduction band, then content at full page width. search Search results Yes The search form and the list of results. landing Landing No A wide introduction band, then content in full-width sections. sidebar Sidebar No Content with a side column for related links and notes. full-width Full width No Content across the whole page width, without a reading column.

items.text: Page shell every page extends. Sets lang and dir on from the page's language, includes the core partial, makes "Skip to main content" the first thing to tab to, and has the landmarks , for each menu and the language switcher, the site's form (partials/search-form.html.twig, when search_action is set), and . Shows messages at the top of through partials/messages.html.twig. The is document_title when set, else the title block and the site name, with "Error: " in front when the form has errors. items.title: Create a theme
items.text:
In this tutorial you make a SightPress theme of your own, "Harbour". You start from the theme template, change its colours, override a template, add a layout, check and preview it, install it on a website, and publish it. You need some experience with the command line, PHP and CSS. The template already has everything a theme needs, and the checks tell you in words when something isn't right.

You need:

  • PHP 8.5 and Composer 2;
  • a SightPress project to try the theme in (see Getting started);
  • for screenshots only: Node.js and Playwright's Chromium (npx playwright install chromium).

items.title: 1. Create your theme from the template
items.text:
composer create-project sightpress/theme-template harbour
cd harbour
composer check

You should see each check pass, ending with:

The theme "My theme" passes: 172 colour pairs checked in light and dark mode, with and without more contrast; the base font size is at least 16 px; the required templates are there; it ships no screenshot.

On GitHub, you can instead open the theme template and choose Use this template, then clone your new repository and run composer install.

items.title: 2. Make it yours
items.text:
A theme has an id: lower-case words joined by hyphens, starting with your vendor name. Ours is acme-harbour.

  1. In composer.json, change name to acme/theme-harbour, and write your own description and homepage.
  2. In src/MyTheme.php, change ID to acme-harbour. Change the name to Harbour and write a description of one or two sentences. Fill in author.
  3. In theme.json, change name to acme-harbour and label to Harbour.
  4. Write previewDescription: what the top of your theme's preview page looks like, for people who can't see its screenshot. Describe the look, not the file. For example: "A dark blue top bar with the site name in white, a pale blue band with a large heading and a yellow Download button."

The template's README lists the rest: renaming the class and its namespace when you want to.

items.title: 3. Change the colours
items.text:
Colours are design tokens in theme.json, one set for light mode and one for dark mode. Try a light blue for buttons and highlights in light mode:

"primary": "#7fb3ff",

Run the checks:

composer check

They fail, and say why:

The theme "Harbour" fails with 3 problems:
1. In light mode, text "on-primary" (#ffffff) on "primary" (#7fb3ff) has a contrast of 2.14:1; it needs at least 4.50:1.
2. In light mode, interface colour "primary" (#7fb3ff) on "background" (#ffffff) has a contrast of 2.14:1; it needs at least 3.00:1.
3. In light mode, interface colour "primary" (#7fb3ff) on "surface" (#f3f4f6) has a contrast of 1.94:1; it needs at least 3.00:1.

White text on a light blue is too hard to read, and the light blue itself is hard to see on the white page. Use a darker blue, and run the checks again:

"primary": "#0b4f8a",

Every colour pair in the contrast section of theme.json is checked in light and dark mode, with and without "more contrast": text needs 4.5:1, borders and other interface colours 3:1. Chart colours are always checked.

items.title: 4. Override a template
items.text:
A theme's templates are in templates/. Change the footer of every page: in templates/master.html.twig, replace the footer block with:

{% block footer %}<p>{{ site_name }}, made with the Harbour theme.</p>{% endblock %}

A template you don't have comes from the default theme, so you only keep the ones you change. Keep the shell's skip link, its landmarks and {% include '@seo/head.html.twig' %}: the checks refuse a shell without that line, because it holds every page's description, canonical address and structured data.

items.title: 5. Add a layout
items.text:
Editors choose a layout for each page. Besides the required ones (default, home, search), a theme can have the standard layouts landing, sidebar and full-width. Add sidebar:

  1. In src/MyTheme.php, list it in the manifest:

    layouts: [...LayoutDefinition::required(), new LayoutDefinition(LayoutDefinition::SIDEBAR, 'Sidebar')],

  2. Create templates/layouts/sidebar.html.twig:

    {% extends 'master.html.twig' %}
{% block title %}{{ title }}{% endblock %}
{% block main %}
{%- set side = block('aside') is defined ? block('aside')|trim : '' %}
<div class="container">
    <h1>{{ title }}</h1>
    {%- if lead is defined and lead is not empty %}<p class="lead">{{ lead }}</p>{% endif %}
    {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    {%- if side %}
    <aside aria-labelledby="page-aside-title">{{ side|raw }}</aside>
    {%- endif %}
</div>
{% endblock %}
{% block aside %}{% endblock %}

SightPress fills the aside block with "In this section", the pages around this one, starting with a heading whose id is page-aside-title. When there's nothing to show, the page has no <aside>. A page whose layout a theme doesn't have is shown in the standard layout, and keeps its own for the next theme that has it.

items.title: 6. Check it
items.text:
composer check

Besides the code style, static analysis and tests, this runs theme:validate, the checks SightPress runs before it applies a theme. It also refuses a screenshot or a build/ folder that would end up in your package.

items.title: 7. Preview it
items.text:
composer preview

Open build/theme-preview/acme-harbour/index.html in any browser. It works offline and needs no PHP. It is the same page for every theme, so you can compare them:

  • a top bar with links to each part of the page;
  • a band with your theme's name, description and a Download button;
  • one block of every kind;
  • the footer.

Go through it with the keyboard alone, at 200% and 400% zoom, in dark mode and with a contrast theme.

With Node.js and Chromium installed, composer preview -- --screenshot also writes screenshot.png, screenshot-dark.png and page.png in the same folder. Use them for your README. Never commit them: your theme's releases get them attached automatically.

items.title: 8. Try it on a website
items.text:
In your SightPress project, add the theme as a path repository, so changes show up as you make them:

composer config repositories.harbour '{"type": "path", "url": "../harbour", "options": {"symlink": true}}'
composer require acme/theme-harbour:@dev
bin/sightpress cache:clear
bin/sightpress theme:validate acme-harbour

Then apply it, from the command line:

bin/sightpress site:theme:apply demo acme-harbour

or in the admin panel, under Appearance: choose Use Harbour. If pages use a layout your theme doesn't have, SightPress lists them first. To see the screenshot in the theme picker, run bin/sightpress theme:publish-assets.

items.title: 9. Open a pull request
items.text:
Push your theme to GitHub and open a pull request with a change. The template's workflows add two things:

  • a download: the preview page, its screenshots and an accessibility report, in one zip;
  • a comment on the pull request with the download link, your previewDescription and the accessibility result in light mode, dark mode and forced colours.

A reviewer can judge the change without installing anything (see Review a theme change).

items.title: 10. Publish it
items.text:
1. Merge your pull requests. Release Please keeps a release pull request open; merging it tags the release and attaches the preview and the screenshots to it.
  2. Submit your repository on packagist.org and turn on its GitHub hook (or add the PACKAGIST_USERNAME and PACKAGIST_API_TOKEN secrets the release workflow uses).
  3. Anyone running SightPress can now install your theme with composer require acme/theme-harbour.

That's it: you have made, checked, previewed, applied and published a theme.
